text: You're given equations like A divided by B equals a value, for pairs of variables, plus a list of queries, C divided by D. Return each query's value, or negative one if it can't be determined from the equations.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — if I know a over b and b over c, I can chain them: a over c equals a over b times b over c. So this is really a graph where variables are nodes and each equation is a weighted edge. Is that the intended model?
Exactly. What about the negative one cases?

Two of them. If either variable never appears in the equations, it's undefined, so negative one. And if both are defined but lie in disconnected parts of the graph, there's no path, so negative one. Notably x over x for an undefined x is negative one, not one — I have to check is it in the graph before the equal-variable shortcut.
Good catch. Inputs are valid — no contradictions, no division by zero.
Let me run through an example. A over b is two, b over c is three. Then a over c is two times three, six; b over a is one half; a over a is one; and a over e is negative one, since e is undefined.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. This problem reminds me of path search on a weighted graph, where the answer is the product of the edge weights along the path. I build a directed weighted graph: a over b equals v gives an edge a to b of weight v, and b to a of weight one over v. Each query C over D becomes: find any path from C to D and multiply the edge weights — the intermediate variables telescope away, leaving C over D. I'll do a BFS per query carrying a running product. With at most twenty equations and twenty queries, that's trivially fast.

Here's the plan. One: build the graph with both the forward edge and its reciprocal. Two: for each query, if either variable isn't in the graph, return negative one; if they're equal, return one. Three: BFS from the start with a running product, and when the end shows up as a neighbor, return the product times that edge; if the queue empties, return negative one. One thing worth flagging — the running product starts at one, the multiplicative identity, and gets multiplied by each edge weight. And the ordering of the guards matters — the not-in-graph check must come before the start-equals-end shortcut, so an undefined x over x correctly returns negative one. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. Each equation stores a over b as v and b over a as one over v. Each query calls a BFS helper: the two guards in that order, then a queue of node and product, seeded with the start at one. A neighbor that's the end returns right away; a new one is marked and pushed with the product times the edge weight. One thing worth flagging — on a hit I return w times nw, not just w: the last edge's weight is part of the answer. And returning on the first hit is safe, because with consistent inputs every path gives the same product.

Let's dry-run on a over b equals two and b over c equals three, across a few queries. A over c goes a, then b with product two, then c with two times three, so six. B over a is one half, and a over a is one. The rows that matter are the last two: a over e and x over x both return negative one because the variable is undefined — and crucially x over x is not one, since the in-graph guard runs before the equal-variable shortcut.

Time is q times V plus E — one BFS per query over the graph. Space is V plus E for the adjacency map, plus the visited set and queue. Oh, one more thing — if there were far more queries than variables, I'd precompute all pairs once, Floyd-Warshall style: V cubed to build and constant time per query. Or I'd use a weighted union-find storing each node's ratio to its root. And if the input could contradict, that weighted union-find would let me detect it while building.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You modeled division as a weighted graph and saw the telescoping product. You built both the forward and reciprocal edges. And you nailed the guard ordering so an undefined x over x returns negative one rather than one. Good work.
